title: Why do we eat spicy food
paragraphs: You know the feeling – your ears start to warm up, your tongue goes numb, you start sweating and taking deep breaths. You've just eaten something spicy knowing it would be painful, and, yet, you chose to do it anyway. Are humans just masochistic, or is there something else going on? The answer lies in both science and history.

Let's start with the science. Spicy isn't actually a taste like salty, sweet, sour and bitter – it’s a sensation. This sensation is triggered by a chemical compound found in chilli peppers called 'capsaicin'. When we eat foods containing capsaicin, our bodies are tricked into thinking the temperature is actually rising. In trying to temper the burning sensation, our bodies release endorphins which control pain and, at the same time, give a feeling of pleasure – like painkillers.

This is what is happening chemically, but there is also a conscious side to choosing spicy food. Dr Tamara Rosenbaum, Cognitive Neuroscientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, explains in an interview with the BBC that this is because we are rational beings – we know that the burning sensation of chilli does not physically harm us. Furthermore, we derive pleasure from the other ingredients chilli is generally cooked and eaten with – including fat, sugar and salt. So – like skydiving – eating chilli is a form of thrill-seeking or 'benign masochism', where we get pleasure from a seemingly negative sensation.

This masochistic relationship with capsaicin has been a long one, starting in the Andes of South America, where chilli peppers originate. Humans were one of the few mammals on Earth that developed a taste for capsaicin so, archaeological evidence suggests, they started cultivating chilli peppers about six thousand years ago. Human intervention changed the chilli pepper to suit human tastes and needs – including the pepper's colour, size and capsaicin content – helping to explain the many different types of chilli peppers now available.

Fast-forward to today, and our love affair with the chilli pepper is going strong. We eat around 57.3 million tons of peppers globally each year, and chilli is a key ingredient in traditional dishes from Mexico to Korea. Maybe we are masochistic after all.

sentences.english: You know the feeling – your ears start to warm up, your tongue goes numb, you start sweating and taking deep breaths.
sentences.chinese: 你懂这种感觉——耳朵开始发烫，舌头发麻，浑身出汗，同时还深呼吸。

sentences.english: You've just eaten something spicy knowing it would be painful, and, yet, you chose to do it anyway.
sentences.chinese: 你明知吃辛辣食物会难受，却还是选择去吃。

sentences.english: Are humans just masochistic, or is there something else going on?
sentences.chinese: 人类只是有受虐倾向吗，还是另有原因？

sentences.english: The answer lies in both science and history.
sentences.chinese: 答案藏在科学与历史之中。
我们先从科学角度说起。

sentences.english: Spicy isn't actually a taste like salty, sweet, sour and bitter – it’s a sensation.
sentences.chinese: 辛辣其实并非咸、甜、酸、苦那样的味觉，而是一种感官感受。

sentences.english: This sensation is triggered by a chemical compound found in chilli peppers called 'capsaicin'.
sentences.chinese: 这种感受由辣椒中一种名为“辣椒素”的化合物触发。

sentences.english: When we eat foods containing capsaicin, our bodies are tricked into thinking the temperature is actually rising.
sentences.chinese: 当我们食用含有辣椒素的食物时，身体会误以为体温在升高。

sentences.english: In trying to temper the burning sensation, our bodies release endorphins which control pain and, at the same time, give a feeling of pleasure – like painkillers.
sentences.chinese: 为了缓解灼烧感，身体会释放内啡肽，这种物质既能镇痛，又能带来愉悦感，效果如同止痛药。

sentences.english: This is what is happening chemically, but there is also a conscious side to choosing spicy food.
sentences.chinese: 这是生理层面的化学反应，但选择吃辣还有主观意识层面的原因。

sentences.english: Dr Tamara Rosenbaum, Cognitive Neuroscientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, explains in an interview with the BBC that this is because we are rational beings – we know that the burning sensation of chilli does not physically harm us.
sentences.chinese: 墨西哥国立自治大学的认知神经科学家塔玛拉·罗森鲍姆博士在接受BBC采访时解释道，这是因为人类是理性生物——我们清楚辣椒带来的灼烧感并不会对身体造成实质伤害。

sentences.english: Furthermore, we derive pleasure from the other ingredients chilli is generally cooked and eaten with – including fat, sugar and salt.
sentences.chinese: 此外，我们还能从与辣椒一同烹制食用的其他食材中获得愉悦感，比如脂肪、糖和盐。

sentences.english: So – like skydiving – eating chilli is a form of thrill-seeking or 'benign masochism', where we get pleasure from a seemingly negative sensation.
sentences.chinese: 所以，就像跳伞一样，吃辣是一种寻求刺激的行为，或是“良性受虐”，即从看似负面的感官感受中获得快乐。

sentences.english: This masochistic relationship with capsaicin has been a long one, starting in the Andes of South America, where chilli peppers originate.
sentences.chinese: 人类与辣椒素的这种“受虐式”渊源由来已久，起源于南美洲的安第斯山脉，那里也是辣椒的原产地。

sentences.english: Humans were one of the few mammals on Earth that developed a taste for capsaicin so, archaeological evidence suggests, they started cultivating chilli peppers about six thousand years ago.
sentences.chinese: 考古证据表明，人类是地球上少数能接受辣椒素的哺乳动物之一，大约六千年前就开始种植辣椒。

sentences.english: Human intervention changed the chilli pepper to suit human tastes and needs – including the pepper's colour, size and capsaicin content – helping to explain the many different types of chilli peppers now available.
sentences.chinese: 人类的干预改造了辣椒，使其适配人类的口味与需求，比如辣椒的颜色、大小和辣椒素含量，这也解释了如今为何会有种类繁多的辣椒。

sentences.english: Fast-forward to today, and our love affair with the chilli pepper is going strong.
sentences.chinese: 时间快进到如今，我们对辣椒的热爱愈发浓烈。

sentences.english: We eat around 57.3 million tons of peppers globally each year, and chilli is a key ingredient in traditional dishes from Mexico to Korea.
sentences.chinese: 全球每年的辣椒消费量约为5730万吨，从墨西哥到韩国，辣椒都是传统菜肴中的关键食材。

sentences.english: Maybe we are masochistic after all.
sentences.chinese: 或许我们终究是有点受虐倾向吧。
